{"slots": {"question": [{"claim": "Does substance use, along with other individual characteristics, shape friendship network formation in AI-majority reservation schools, where prior work has mostly studied racially heterogeneous schools?", "quotes": [{"text": "the role of substance use and other individual characteristics in friendship network formation within AI-majority reservation schools remains understudied", "page": 1}]}],
"central_claim": [{"claim": "In AI-majority reservation schools, friendship ties are organized around structural processes and demographic commonalities rather than risky behaviors. Substance use, depression and AI identity show no consistent association with friendship formation.", "quotes": [{"text": "peer ties are organized around structural and demographic commonalities rather than risky behaviors.", "page": 1}]}],
"evidence": [{"claim": "Cross-sectional network survey of 9th- and 10th-grade students in three schools on one Northern Plains reservation, analysed with exponential random graph models. The paper reports N = 247 in the abstract and a total of 263 in the Methods.", "quotes": [{"text": "Using social network data from 9th and 10th-grade students (N = 247) across three schools on a Northern Plains reservation, we employed exponential random graph models (ERGMs)", "page": 1}, {"text": "for a total sample size of 263.", "page": 6}]}, {"claim": "Substance use was self-reported as binary alcohol, tobacco and marijuana items. Depression was measured with a six-item CES-D scale and AI identity with six items adapted from the MEIM affirmation subscale. Missing substance-use values were imputed from peer perceptions.", "quotes": [{"text": "The survey also included a measure of depression, utilizing the Center for Epidemiologic", "page": 7}, {"text": "The measurement of AI identity was assessed using six items adapted from the Affirmation and Belonging subscale of the Multigroup Ethnic Identity Measure (MEIM) [39].", "page": 7}]}],
"key_findings": [{"claim": "Reciprocity was positive and highly significant in every model, so mutual friendship nominations were a robust structural tendency across the schools.", "quotes": [{"text": "Reciprocity was positive and highly significant in every model, indicating a robust tendency for mutual friendship nominations.", "page": 13}]}, {"claim": "Substance use showed no consistent or robust association with friendship dynamics in the sample, including sender, receiver and homophily effects.", "quotes": [{"text": "Substance use demonstrated no consistent or robust association with friendship dynamics in this sample.", "page": 13}]}, {"claim": "The only substance-use effect reported was an alcohol sender effect in School C. The authors describe the isolated effects as not replicating across schools or substances.", "quotes": [{"text": "The only exception was a positive sender effect for alcohol use in School C (AME = 0.015, p < 0.05)", "page": 13}]}, {"claim": "AI identity was largely unassociated with sending or receiving ties, with only a borderline positive receiver effect in School C. Depression effects were negligible in magnitude.", "quotes": [{"text": "AI identity was largely unassociated with sending or receiving ties, with only a borderline positive receiver effect in School C.", "page": 13}]}, {"claim": "Gender and grade homophily were strong and significant in all three schools, which the authors read as the main axes of friendship formation.", "quotes": [{"text": "Strong and significant homophily was present for gender and grade across all schools, indicating that shared gender identity and grade level are primary axes of friendship formation.", "page": 13}]}],
"scope_and_limits": [{"claim": "The results cover only three schools on one reservation and may not extend to AI youth in racially heterogeneous schools.", "quotes": [{"text": "the results presented here represent only three schools on one reservation", "page": 16}]}, {"claim": "The cross-sectional design cannot separate selection from influence, so the findings are associations and not evidence of causal effects of substance use, depression or AI identity on friendship.", "quotes": [{"text": "formation, not as evidence that substance use, depression, or AI identity causally affect friendship formation", "page": 17}]}],
"theoretical_positioning": [{"claim": "The authors extend the ERGM endogenous-effects framework by arguing that its parameters are culturally shaped. They treat the framework as applicable but not culturally neutral in AI reservation settings.", "quotes": [{"text": "Critically, their prevalence and strength are not culturally neutral but are shaped by the social norms and relational expectations of a community", "page": 3}]}],
"interlocutor_claim": [{"claim": "The authors dispute the claim from research in diverse school settings that substance use is linked to friendship ties through selection and influence. They test whether this holds where students are predominantly AI and find it does not.", "quotes": [{"text": "Research in diverse school settings has consistently demonstrated that substance use is linked to friendship ties, often through processes of selection", "page": 2}]}]}}
